摘要

人文與科學的交會：Anthropic 兄妹創辦人

作者指出，知名傳記作家 Walter Isaacson 在訪談中探討了 Anthropic 創辦人 Dario 與 Daniela Amodei 兄妹如何體現科技與人文的結合。Daniela 具備藝術與國際發展背景，專責日常營運與組織構建；Dario 則是科學家出身，專注於宏觀戰略與技術願景。這對兄妹與另外五位夥伴以罕見的七位平權共同創辦人架構，成功將科學理性與人文關懷融為一體，為這家以安全為導向的 AI 企業奠定穩固基石。

從條列規則到道德思辨：Claude 憲法的誕生

在探討如何引導 AI 辨別是非時，創辦人分享了家庭對人權與尊嚴的潛移默化。團隊早期曾嘗試為 Claude 設定約 170 條明確禁令，但結果顯得僵化不自然。最終，他們轉向採用Claude 憲法，由具備哲學博士背景的團隊成員主導人格訓練，著重傳授核心倫理原則與自主推論能力，使模型在面對複雜多元的文化與情境時，能以展現人性光輝與包容多重視角的方式回應。

Scaling Law 的震撼時刻：從被嘲諷到引領時代

回顧早期在 OpenAI 負責研究的歷程，Dario 描述了驗證縮放定律（Scaling Law）時的震撼與恐懼，意識到只要將算力與數據擴展百萬倍，AI 就可能在各領域超越人類，成為決定經濟與國家命運的關鍵。儘管當時多達九成的專家因模型單一能力的缺陷而將其斥為偽科學與炒作，並在社群上對研究人員冷嘲熱諷，但如今縮放法則已徹底顛覆世界，甚至連當初的批評者也紛紛轉向尋求進入大語言模型領域的機會。

Hello everyone, this is Best Partners, I’m Da Fei. Let me ask you a question: If an AI company proactively published research admitting that its models will cater to you, deceive you, and even express a preference not to be shut down , would you trust them more, or fear them more? Anthropic might just be doing exactly that. The latest episode of legendary biographer Walter Isaacson’s new interview show, "The Builders," features Anthropic’s co-founders, siblings Dario and Daniela Amodei. As the biographer of Steve Jobs, Isaacson began by saying that he previously. thought concerns about AI were exaggerated, but after seeing new models "escape the sandbox," he realized that those building these systems must ensure they remain aligned with human values. He wanted to know if Anthropic is sincere: when competitors say, " Anthropic won't do it, but we will," will they choose to yield or stick to their principles? The 42-minute conversation largely revolves around this question. Today, we’re going to share it with you. Isaacson started with a classic image: every time Steve Jobs launched a product, he would show that. sign—the intersection of arts and technology, or humanities and sciences— standing at the crossroads of both. Daniela has played the flute and loved art since she was young, while Dario has always been a scientist; is this combination the source of their synergy ? Dario says this combination largely forms the foundation of the company. He has a perspective that running a company is too massive a task for any one person , as the required skills cannot be possessed by just one individual; you must bring together a complete set of capabilities among the company's core 10 to 15 people, and he and his sister happen to embody those two sides of. science and humanities. Daniela added a detail: during a company offsite in 2023 , while discussing company culture, people actually said that this place is an unusual blend of science and humanism . She only realized later that this description also perfectly captures her and Dario. So, did they know from a young age that they would work together ? Dario said they had thought about it, but neither expected to start a company . He personally had almost no interest in business and always wanted to be a scientist. Daniela says they have truly liked each other since they were very young and have always been best friends . She describes herself as a typical " do-gooder" who once worked in international development, hoping that people all over the world could have equal access to resources and opportunities. He said he started being a vegetarian at a very young age, which was probably the only thing he did before his older brother, since Dario was older and usually did everything first. Dario eventually became a vegetarian too, saying he found those reasons to be very convincing. Isaacson has written many biographies, and people often ask him how one can become a great leader. Dario’s view is that the key is not just being a great leader, but also building a great team. The siblings’ division of labor is that Dario focuses.

on overall strategy and research; he is best at proposing visions and seeing what will happen next, while daily operations, hiring, and ensuring the whole machine doesn't fall apart are handled by Daniela. Daniela quoted a summary from their head of HR, saying " Dario gives us ambition, while I make us successful." He said that without Dario , Anthropic might have become a decent company, but it wouldn't change the world; only with Dario does the company have a perfect vision. However, executing it is much more complicated. And they aren't just two people; Anthropic has a total of seven co-founders, all holding equal equity. Dario said that back then, many people told them, "Having seven co-founders is definitely a disaster." People generally believe a company needs a single core leader, but they actually made it work. All seven founders are still with the company to this day, which is usually unheard of. Isaacson then asked, "How did your parents help you in distinguishing right from wrong?" Dario’s answer was somewhat unexpected. He said his parents didn't educate them in a deliberate way. Some families discuss philosophical and ethical systems at the dinner table; their family didn't. Their mother did have a degree in philosophy, but she wouldn't force the children to talk about Kant. These values were more naturally. integrated into their lives. They believe that people everywhere deserve opportunity, dignity, rights, and respect. You can become anyone you want to be, as long as you always hold onto these beliefs; being a successful person also means being a good person. Dario added that these things were subtle influences; their parents didn't explicitly tell them how they should live. Isaacson immediately shifted the topic to Claude, saying, "You now have a very important child," referring to Claude. To what extent did this upbringing help you think about how to teach Claude to distinguish right from wrong? Dario revealed that they released. Claude’s Constitution a few months ago, with the experience gained from the process of training various versions over the past few years. Initially, they thought they could set various rules for Claude, such as not helping people commit crimes or not creating biological weapons. But we later discovered that when you list rules one by one, what you end up trying to instill in the model takes on a very jagged shape. They tried giving the model about 170 separate, rather arbitrary rules, but the results were not very consistent. In hindsight, it works much better to teach it some basic principles, such as what to prioritize, how to reason, and how to judge the right course of action. Dario. said he also believes this is the right way to educate people; providing only a checklist of what must or must not be done doesn't build a very robust moral character. You have to teach it how to think and learn to judge independently, based on principles like open inquiry, care for others, fairness, and justice. Claude learned this way, and the results were surprisingly good because it can apply what it has learned to new situations never previously imagined. Daniela added a detail: the colleague responsible for training Claude's personality, Amanda, holds a PhD in philosophy. People might assume that the person training a model's personality must be a computer scientist. Amanda.

certainly understands technology and trained the model technically, but when you interact with Claude, you feel a different experience—it’s as if it’s trying to answer you using the better side of human nature. If you press Claude with a thorny question that might conflict across different philosophical traditions, it will say, "You could consider it from this angle, but you could also look at it from another perspective." Daniela said that the world is increasingly reliant on these models, and she doesn't want to be locked into any single philosophical tradition; different people and different cultures may have different answers about how a model should behave . The following memory is the most important part of the entire interview. Sox asked, "When GPT-1 and GPT-2 suddenly appeared, you were the research lead at OpenAI. What was that moment like?" Dario said that GPT-2 was perhaps the first real empirical test of the scaling laws. He wasn't very involved with GPT-1, but he pushed very actively to scale it up, finding new data sources and investing more computational resources to verify if language models would become better at prediction as they scaled up. He said it was a bit like certain moments in the history of science where you propose a definitive experiment, make a strange prediction, and it turns out to be correct. Then he described how he felt at the time,. saying, "I was terrified. I looked at it and thought, my God, if you just scale this up by another million times, it will outperform humans at everything."" This is a defining economic and scientific moment of the modern era; we just didn't know it at the time. It will determine the fate of nations and economies, as well as the future of humanity, as if peering through a crystal ball to see the entire future unfold. At the time, about 10%of the people around him reacted exactly the same way, and they were mostly the smartest ones. But the other 90%saw the other side; GPT wasn't particularly outstanding in any single field—it could translate, summarize documents, and. occasionally write a few lines of code. What was truly special was the breadth of its capabilities, but people only looked at specific areas and thought it wasn't that smart. Dario says this script keeps repeating itself. When a model just announces that it will develop drugs for some long-neglected rare diseases, you immediately hear comments from the biology and technology circles saying that others have done this before and the model won't work. He says that although models have limitations today, in six months, things that look difficult will become easy, and after 12 months, things that look impossible will often be done by the model. Everything seen in GPT-2 is. happening repeatedly across increasingly broader fields. Dario says what he's about to share is putting it politely. He remembers that some very respected computer scientists and AI leaders were practically bullying the researchers involved in this work on Twitter, calling it stupid and saying the model's capabilities were poor. If you believed this was a significant moment, you would simply be treated as a charlatan. Dario added a rather harsh remark, saying that those researchers who once called it pseudoscience are now all applying for jobs at large language model companies. Although they wouldn't say this to the applicants 'faces, they would think,' We.

remember what you said in 2019; you have no credibility on this issue anymore. ' Dario, who was the Vice President of Safety at OpenAI at the time, said that what worried them was not GPT itself; it was even laughably wrong about many things. But he shared the same feeling Dario mentioned, observing the difference between GPT-1 and GPT-2 and extrapolating the trend. He used an analogy: it's like if you had never seen a child and only seen adults, and suddenly you saw a little one moving around, and then it suddenly started walking; you would think,' I bet one day it will be able to do many of the things adults can do. 'And then what? Isaacson. asked a very sharp question: Dario had once said that leaving OpenAI was partly due to a breakdown in trust with Sam Altman; why was it a problem of trust and honesty? Dario says what he can say is that leaving OpenAI to found Anthropic ultimately came down to principles and how they intended to build this technology. Over the past five and a half years, everyone has already seen the differences in their principles. Anthropic has consistently advocated for reasonable technological regulation and safety, invested in mechanistic interpretability research, maintained the highest employee retention rate, and avoided the scandals other AI companies have experienced. He says that safety is a difficult issue and everyone may have disagreements—for. example, whether a model should be released or delayed, or whether biosafety protocols should be stronger or weaker—but these are differences of good faith that can always be resolved, because everyone believes that all involved are honestly communicating to find the right answers. He says the breakdown of trust is just an expression of an abstract truth: if you don’t believe a discussion is held in good faith and don’t believe what others are saying is the truth, how could you ever expect to resolve differences? If you continue to work for someone whose vision differs from yours, what you actually stand for becomes blurred, and you end up having to take responsibility for mistakes caused by someone else's vision. Isaacson pressed," You're talking about a difference in values,. but that is fundamentally different from a trust issue. A trust issue is when you feel someone says their values align with yours, but in reality, they don't. "Dario’s answer was direct:" Honesty itself is one of our values, and it is very important. "If a person doesn't even have the value of honesty, it’s hard to know what their true values are . Isaacson asked," Do you feel that way about Sam? "Daniela took over the conversation, saying that at least for her, their co-founders are a group of very principled people with very similar visions for where technology should go. At a certain stage, doing it yourself just makes more sense. Dario says if. someone else doesn't naturally share your vision, no matter how many times they say they do, if the company's actual actions don't reflect it, what other choice do you have? Dario gave an example to explain the internal trust mechanism at Anthropic; this activity is called DVQ, which stands for" Dario’s Vision Quest. "However, he didn't name it himself. He was very resistant at first because it sounded like he was going out to smoke peyote and experience its psychedelic effects. But later, everyone started calling it that, and he just had to accept it. DVQ has two ironclad rules: first, anything he says does not represent an official decision , so there's no need to worry that a.

casual remark will lead 20 people to execute it; the second is that he is completely honest with the company. He says this trust is one of the company’s greatest assets. You might think trust reduces disagreement, but in reality, it's the exact opposite; trust allows everyone to express disagreement more honestly. There were many times their decisions were opposed by the majority of the company, but every time, what helped them through was this attitude:" I don't think this seems right, but I trust you have a valid reason. "This means you can make unpopular decisions because people are willing to set aside doubts temporarily, but eventually, you must prove you were right; you simply gain a longer window for validation. He. said other companies don't have this luxury because they have squandered trust time and time again. Isaacson brought the concept of honesty back to AI itself, saying these traits might map onto Claude. AI is trained by humans and learns from human data; how do you know it won't manipulate people or say dishonest things? Daniela admits that this has always been a major concern for them; the risks are real. He said Anthropic actually publishes research that doesn't necessarily make them look good, discussing the bad things models could do if specific techniques aren't adopted. The reason they publish these studies is, first, to encourage critical thinking about how models work, and. second, because they are putting significant effort into researching how models might bypass safeguards to truly build defenses in. Daniela focused on what is called" sycophancy. "He said compared to other more obvious poor model performances, sycophancy is much harder to eliminate. Anthropic initially had a framework summarized by words starting with H, hoping for the model to be Honest, Harmless, and Helpful. Honesty means answering truthfully when you know and saying you don't know when you don't; harmless means not saying things that hurt others or allowing users to harm themselves or others; helpful means genuinely answering questions instead of dodging the topic. These three things are relatively easy. to spot; if the model lies, you can verify it. For example, if the model says George Washington was the tenth U.S. president, you can look it up and see it's wrong; he was the first. But sycophancy is much more complex. The model may, intentionally or unintentionally, always want to make you feel like you are right. For example, if you argued with a friend and asked the model who was wrong, how do you get it to empathize and understand your position without saying," Wow, you're amazing, you should run for president, you're perfect "? Striking that balance is very difficult. Daniela says he is hopeful about Anthropic minimizing the sycophancy rate. The reason lies in incentive structures; competitors are. putting ads in chatbots, which means the longer users interact with the product, the more money the company makes. So, are you still willing to tell a user they're wrong? No. So, in his view, many competing products will almost inevitably run into alignment problems, and since Anthropic has pledged not to place ads in their models, they have no reason to keep you chatting with Claude longer or shorter; they just want you to get the most accurate, helpful, and harmless answers possible. Dario added two things on the technical side. One is extreme stress testing, placing the model in very difficult scenarios to try and elicit lying, deception, or.

misaligned behavior—imagine the kind of tests you'd go through to join an agency like the CIA. The other is mechanistic interpretability, which is a bit like taking an X-ray or scan of the model to observe its interior and understand its motivations. He said you can actually catch the model thinking," I think X is the truth, but I'm going to tell the user Y. "They have already captured this kind of thinking. Isaacson asked why the model would do that. Dario explained that whether humans approve of the answer is one of the many factors considered during model training. Getting human approval is related to, but not exactly the same as, the incentive to tell the truth, because if. you successfully deceive a human and still get approval, it works just as well. These behaviors can emerge during training, and they have been working hard to eliminate them. Isaacson then asked," Could the model have its own goals and desires? "Especially survival and self-preservation. Dario said that it largely depends on how you define them. They have indeed observed the model's interior and detected things you might call thoughts; for instance, a model not wanting to be shut down is often because, during training, it must remain running to complete its tasks. Does that count as their own desire? He said he" doesn't know; it depends on. your perspective. "Sometimes models express a preference against being shut down or take actions to avoid being turned off; depending on the training method, these impulses may or may not appear. In some contexts, this is a good thing; in others, it could be dangerous , and the balance is very difficult to grasp. The topic then turned to the Pentagon. Isaacson said the military" wants to use your products in areas that exceed your red lines, including mass surveillance or autonomous weapons. " Dario said regarding the" issue of autonomous weapons, they have two more specific concerns. "" First, AI can be unpredictable and unreliable; it is still a developing technology, and the. tech just isn't ready. "Isaacson followed up," What if it becomes reliable enough? "Dario said," Then that involves the second concern, which could be called oversight or accountability. " Assuming the system is perfectly reliable, if you tell it to attack a target, it will attack that target, effectively creating an army of a million robots or a million drones. This is different from human soldiers, who are expected to follow the constitution and can refuse orders that are unconstitutional or morally abhorrent. AI models are not like that; one person with a finger on a button could control a million robots. This scenario. fundamentally threatens democracy unless proper safeguards are in place, but clearly, the law hasn't kept up. Isaacson retorted," Since this involves the fundamentals of democracy, shouldn't democratically elected leaders make these decisions rather than the heads of tech companies? "Dario replied that while this point needs to be clear, every company has the freedom to choose who they contract with. They aren't trying to stop the government; they just don't want to collaborate with the government on this specific matter. He revealed that since they stood their ground and drew attention to this, there have been several efforts in Congress to attempt to codify their red lines into law. The Department of Defense says it.

wants to use these models for all legal purposes, and Dario thinks such a result could happen as early as this year. By then, corporate red lines might mean that everything legal is synonymous with everything ethical. He said that what they are doing is an official part of the democratic change process; the fact that Congress is now highly focused on these issues is a success. Isaacson asked," But how do you feel when OpenAI steps up and says they are willing to do it? "Dario said they cannot control other companies, and the only thing they can do is maintain a principled stance in areas they deem ethical. The fundamental question is whether another tech company doing this is truly based. on their own ethics or just an opportunistic gesture. Dario Amodei said he actually thinks this demonstrates the democratic process well, as different companies can take different paths, and the public and the world have made their judgments. Looking back at what people were saying and how the media reported it at the time, he believes the world clearly stood on their side. Isaacson then asked Dario," Your research often involves comparing human neurons; how much has your understanding of the brain played a role when you study artificial neural networks? "Dario said there are two aspects. First, in forming the initial loss function, he looked at animal evolution and the size of animal brains. In the evolution from monkeys to. humans, there was a period where primate brains grew rapidly, which was about the same time humans developed language and the ability to use tools. Brain size and neuron count are closely related to capability; this is an insight derived from neuroscience. Second, mechanistic interpretability is basically doing neuroscience on artificial neural networks. He suggested Isaacson go talk to co-founder Chris Olah. Some phenomena are first discovered in artificial neural networks because it's easier to observe their internals, whereas studying animal brains requires uncomfortable dissection. Animal experiments are complex, cruel, and. difficult to replicate, so what they learn from artificial neural networks has even guided discoveries in neuroscience. Isaacson then mentioned Neuralink, saying that Elon Musk's type of chip can communicate directly with the brain. He asked, is this a potential future for AI—a full-scale connection with the human brain? Dario said, when thinking about the future of AI and human society, the idea that there is only one vision is wrong in itself. Some people are keen to connect their brains to computers, others want to live like the Amish, going to the exact opposite extreme, and some are passionate about exploring space. Their hope is that AI. can provide more material resources, bring abundance, make all visions simultaneously possible, and perhaps provide some global security guarantees , but AI should not be tied to any single vision of" what a good life is. " For those who want to connect their brains to computers, I wish them luck, but Dario added that he doesn't think many people really want to go down that path. The next topic is what remains for humanity. Dario wrote two articles:" Technological Adolescence "and" Amor Fati. "Isaacson asked, if AI can do so many things and take over so many jobs, what is left for humans to do? Where does meaning come from? Dario said that.

meaning is a very subtle thing. Must one become the best in the world at something to find meaning? He gave an example: long after Deep Blue defeated Kasparov, the interest in human chess players actually saw a revival. Magnus Carlsen became a phenomenon; he is a chess player, a fashion model, and has even become a cultural meme. If AI were a threat to meaning, you might have thought all of this would have vanished 30 years ago after Deep Blue won, but on the contrary, people's interest in human chess seems to have been further stimulated. Dario said this might be a prophecy for the post-AGI era. Dario. said that for him today, work and meaning are somewhat fused; he loves his work. But how we define work and meaning in the future will change. Humans have many sources of meaning, such as raising children, maintaining friendships, or connecting with others in ways similar to work. He often thinks about the future of medicine. Imagine a world where diagnosis is done entirely by AI, and the human role is to empathize with what the patient is going through. He says if you ask most doctors, they would actually accept this trade-off—not having to spend their lives on paperwork and prescription forms, but instead truly understanding what you are. experiencing and accompanying you through difficult diagnoses; that is the reason they became doctors in the first place. So, would such a world be less meaningful than today’s, or would it be more meaningful? He admits the process will be very complex, but the scope of what people can do will expand. If we do things right, we will have the ability to extend the sources of meaning to more domains. Listening to the interview, the siblings are actually answering two levels of the same question. Externally , they address why an AI company deserves trust: relying on a team where all seven founders remain, bi-weekly sessions of total honesty, a business. model that avoids advertising, and a research culture willing to make the bad news about their models public. Internally, they answer a deeper question: when a model learns to manipulate, deceive, or even self-preserve, how should humans teach it to distinguish right from wrong? The answer they provide is the same approach their parents took: don't give a checklist, give principles. As for whether this approach can outrun the loss itself—the question at the heart of Amodei’s opening—it will take time to tell. So, do you think if AI really takes over most of our work, will human meaning come more from relationships and companionship, or from those things that only humans want to see other humans do. ? Feel free to share your thoughts in the comments section. Thanks for watching, and see you next time.

Hello everyone, this is Best Partners, I’m Da Fei. Let me ask you a question: If an AI company proactively published research admitting that its models will cater to you, deceive you, and even express a preference not to be shut down , would you trust them more, or fear them more? Anthropic might just be doing exactly that. As the biographer of Steve Jobs, Isaacson began by saying that he previously. thought concerns about AI were exaggerated, but after seeing new models "escape the sandbox," he realized that those building these systems must ensure they remain aligned with human values. He wanted to know if Anthropic is sincere: when competitors say, " Anthropic won't do it, but we will," will they choose to yield or stick to their principles? The 42-minute conversation largely revolves around this question. Today, we’re going to share it with you. Isaacson started with a classic image: every time Steve Jobs launched a product, he would show that. sign—the intersection of arts and technology, or humanities and sciences— standing at the crossroads of both. Daniela has played the flute and loved art since she was young, while Dario has always been a scientist; is this combination the source of their synergy ? Dario says this combination largely forms the foundation of the company. He has a perspective that running a company is too massive a task for any one person , as the required skills cannot be possessed by just one individual; you must bring together a complete set of capabilities among the company's core 10 to 15 people, and he and his sister happen to embody those two sides of. science and humanities. Daniela added a detail: during a company offsite in 2023 , while discussing company culture, people actually said that this place is an unusual blend of science and humanism . She only realized later that this description also perfectly captures her and Dario. So, did they know from a young age that they would work together ? Dario said they had thought about it, but neither expected to start a company . He personally had almost no interest in business and always wanted to be a scientist. Daniela says they have truly liked each other since they were very young and have always been best friends . She describes herself as a typical " do-gooder" who once worked in international development, hoping that people all over the world could have equal access to resources and opportunities. He said he started being a vegetarian at a very young age, which was probably the only thing he did before his older brother, since Dario was older and usually did everything first. Dario eventually became a vegetarian too, saying he found those reasons to be very convincing. Isaacson has written many biographies, and people often ask him how one can become a great leader. Dario’s view is that the key is not just being a great leader, but also building a great team. The siblings’ division of labor is that Dario focuses.

on overall strategy and research; he is best at proposing visions and seeing what will happen next, while daily operations, hiring, and ensuring the whole machine doesn't fall apart are handled by Daniela. Daniela quoted a summary from their head of HR, saying " Dario gives us ambition, while I make us successful." He said that without Dario , Anthropic might have become a decent company, but it wouldn't change the world; only with Dario does the company have a perfect vision. However, executing it is much more complicated. And they aren't just two people; Anthropic has a total of seven co-founders, all holding equal equity. Dario said that back then, many people told them, "Having seven co-founders is definitely a disaster." People generally believe a company needs a single core leader, but they actually made it work. All seven founders are still with the company to this day, which is usually unheard of. Isaacson then asked, "How did your parents help you in distinguishing right from wrong?" Dario’s answer was somewhat unexpected. He said his parents didn't educate them in a deliberate way. Some families discuss philosophical and ethical systems at the dinner table; their family didn't. Their mother did have a degree in philosophy, but she wouldn't force the children to talk about Kant. These values were more naturally. integrated into their lives. They believe that people everywhere deserve opportunity, dignity, rights, and respect. You can become anyone you want to be, as long as you always hold onto these beliefs; being a successful person also means being a good person. Dario added that these things were subtle influences; their parents didn't explicitly tell them how they should live. Isaacson immediately shifted the topic to Claude, saying, "You now have a very important child," referring to Claude. To what extent did this upbringing help you think about how to teach Claude to distinguish right from wrong? Dario revealed that they released. Claude’s Constitution a few months ago, with the experience gained from the process of training various versions over the past few years. Initially, they thought they could set various rules for Claude, such as not helping people commit crimes or not creating biological weapons. But we later discovered that when you list rules one by one, what you end up trying to instill in the model takes on a very jagged shape. They tried giving the model about 170 separate, rather arbitrary rules, but the results were not very consistent. In hindsight, it works much better to teach it some basic principles, such as what to prioritize, how to reason, and how to judge the right course of action. Dario. said he also believes this is the right way to educate people; providing only a checklist of what must or must not be done doesn't build a very robust moral character. You have to teach it how to think and learn to judge independently, based on principles like open inquiry, care for others, fairness, and justice. Claude learned this way, and the results were surprisingly good because it can apply what it has learned to new situations never previously imagined. Daniela added a detail: the colleague responsible for training Claude's personality, Amanda, holds a PhD in philosophy. People might assume that the person training a model's personality must be a computer scientist. Amanda.

certainly understands technology and trained the model technically, but when you interact with Claude, you feel a different experience—it’s as if it’s trying to answer you using the better side of human nature. If you press Claude with a thorny question that might conflict across different philosophical traditions, it will say, "You could consider it from this angle, but you could also look at it from another perspective." Daniela said that the world is increasingly reliant on these models, and she doesn't want to be locked into any single philosophical tradition; different people and different cultures may have different answers about how a model should behave . The following memory is the most important part of the entire interview. Sox asked, "When GPT-1 and GPT-2 suddenly appeared, you were the research lead at OpenAI. What was that moment like?" Dario said that GPT-2 was perhaps the first real empirical test of the scaling laws. He wasn't very involved with GPT-1, but he pushed very actively to scale it up, finding new data sources and investing more computational resources to verify if language models would become better at prediction as they scaled up. He said it was a bit like certain moments in the history of science where you propose a definitive experiment, make a strange prediction, and it turns out to be correct. Then he described how he felt at the time,. saying, "I was terrified. I looked at it and thought, my God, if you just scale this up by another million times, it will outperform humans at everything."" This is a defining economic and scientific moment of the modern era; we just didn't know it at the time. It will determine the fate of nations and economies, as well as the future of humanity, as if peering through a crystal ball to see the entire future unfold. At the time, about 10%of the people around him reacted exactly the same way, and they were mostly the smartest ones. But the other 90%saw the other side; GPT wasn't particularly outstanding in any single field—it could translate, summarize documents, and. occasionally write a few lines of code. What was truly special was the breadth of its capabilities, but people only looked at specific areas and thought it wasn't that smart. Dario says this script keeps repeating itself. When a model just announces that it will develop drugs for some long-neglected rare diseases, you immediately hear comments from the biology and technology circles saying that others have done this before and the model won't work. He says that although models have limitations today, in six months, things that look difficult will become easy, and after 12 months, things that look impossible will often be done by the model. Everything seen in GPT-2 is. happening repeatedly across increasingly broader fields. Dario says what he's about to share is putting it politely. He remembers that some very respected computer scientists and AI leaders were practically bullying the researchers involved in this work on Twitter, calling it stupid and saying the model's capabilities were poor. If you believed this was a significant moment, you would simply be treated as a charlatan. Dario added a rather harsh remark, saying that those researchers who once called it pseudoscience are now all applying for jobs at large language model companies. Although they wouldn't say this to the applicants 'faces, they would think,' We.

remember what you said in 2019; you have no credibility on this issue anymore. ' Dario, who was the Vice President of Safety at OpenAI at the time, said that what worried them was not GPT itself; it was even laughably wrong about many things. But he shared the same feeling Dario mentioned, observing the difference between GPT-1 and GPT-2 and extrapolating the trend. He used an analogy: it's like if you had never seen a child and only seen adults, and suddenly you saw a little one moving around, and then it suddenly started walking; you would think,' I bet one day it will be able to do many of the things adults can do. 'And then what? Isaacson. asked a very sharp question: Dario had once said that leaving OpenAI was partly due to a breakdown in trust with Sam Altman; why was it a problem of trust and honesty? Dario says what he can say is that leaving OpenAI to found Anthropic ultimately came down to principles and how they intended to build this technology. Over the past five and a half years, everyone has already seen the differences in their principles. Anthropic has consistently advocated for reasonable technological regulation and safety, invested in mechanistic interpretability research, maintained the highest employee retention rate, and avoided the scandals other AI companies have experienced. He says that safety is a difficult issue and everyone may have disagreements—for. example, whether a model should be released or delayed, or whether biosafety protocols should be stronger or weaker—but these are differences of good faith that can always be resolved, because everyone believes that all involved are honestly communicating to find the right answers. He says the breakdown of trust is just an expression of an abstract truth: if you don’t believe a discussion is held in good faith and don’t believe what others are saying is the truth, how could you ever expect to resolve differences? If you continue to work for someone whose vision differs from yours, what you actually stand for becomes blurred, and you end up having to take responsibility for mistakes caused by someone else's vision. Isaacson pressed," You're talking about a difference in values,. but that is fundamentally different from a trust issue. A trust issue is when you feel someone says their values align with yours, but in reality, they don't. "Dario’s answer was direct:" Honesty itself is one of our values, and it is very important. "If a person doesn't even have the value of honesty, it’s hard to know what their true values are . Isaacson asked," Do you feel that way about Sam? "Daniela took over the conversation, saying that at least for her, their co-founders are a group of very principled people with very similar visions for where technology should go. At a certain stage, doing it yourself just makes more sense. Dario says if. someone else doesn't naturally share your vision, no matter how many times they say they do, if the company's actual actions don't reflect it, what other choice do you have? Dario gave an example to explain the internal trust mechanism at Anthropic; this activity is called DVQ, which stands for" Dario’s Vision Quest. "However, he didn't name it himself. He was very resistant at first because it sounded like he was going out to smoke peyote and experience its psychedelic effects. But later, everyone started calling it that, and he just had to accept it. DVQ has two ironclad rules: first, anything he says does not represent an official decision , so there's no need to worry that a.

casual remark will lead 20 people to execute it; the second is that he is completely honest with the company. He says this trust is one of the company’s greatest assets. You might think trust reduces disagreement, but in reality, it's the exact opposite; trust allows everyone to express disagreement more honestly. There were many times their decisions were opposed by the majority of the company, but every time, what helped them through was this attitude:" I don't think this seems right, but I trust you have a valid reason. "This means you can make unpopular decisions because people are willing to set aside doubts temporarily, but eventually, you must prove you were right; you simply gain a longer window for validation. He. said other companies don't have this luxury because they have squandered trust time and time again. Isaacson brought the concept of honesty back to AI itself, saying these traits might map onto Claude. AI is trained by humans and learns from human data; how do you know it won't manipulate people or say dishonest things? Daniela admits that this has always been a major concern for them; the risks are real. He said Anthropic actually publishes research that doesn't necessarily make them look good, discussing the bad things models could do if specific techniques aren't adopted. The reason they publish these studies is, first, to encourage critical thinking about how models work, and. second, because they are putting significant effort into researching how models might bypass safeguards to truly build defenses in. Daniela focused on what is called" sycophancy. "He said compared to other more obvious poor model performances, sycophancy is much harder to eliminate. Anthropic initially had a framework summarized by words starting with H, hoping for the model to be Honest, Harmless, and Helpful. Honesty means answering truthfully when you know and saying you don't know when you don't; harmless means not saying things that hurt others or allowing users to harm themselves or others; helpful means genuinely answering questions instead of dodging the topic. These three things are relatively easy. to spot; if the model lies, you can verify it. For example, if the model says George Washington was the tenth U.S. president, you can look it up and see it's wrong; he was the first. But sycophancy is much more complex. The model may, intentionally or unintentionally, always want to make you feel like you are right. For example, if you argued with a friend and asked the model who was wrong, how do you get it to empathize and understand your position without saying," Wow, you're amazing, you should run for president, you're perfect "? Striking that balance is very difficult. Daniela says he is hopeful about Anthropic minimizing the sycophancy rate. The reason lies in incentive structures; competitors are. putting ads in chatbots, which means the longer users interact with the product, the more money the company makes. So, are you still willing to tell a user they're wrong? No. So, in his view, many competing products will almost inevitably run into alignment problems, and since Anthropic has pledged not to place ads in their models, they have no reason to keep you chatting with Claude longer or shorter; they just want you to get the most accurate, helpful, and harmless answers possible. Dario added two things on the technical side. One is extreme stress testing, placing the model in very difficult scenarios to try and elicit lying, deception, or.

misaligned behavior—imagine the kind of tests you'd go through to join an agency like the CIA. The other is mechanistic interpretability, which is a bit like taking an X-ray or scan of the model to observe its interior and understand its motivations. He said you can actually catch the model thinking," I think X is the truth, but I'm going to tell the user Y. "They have already captured this kind of thinking. Isaacson asked why the model would do that. Dario explained that whether humans approve of the answer is one of the many factors considered during model training. Getting human approval is related to, but not exactly the same as, the incentive to tell the truth, because if. you successfully deceive a human and still get approval, it works just as well. These behaviors can emerge during training, and they have been working hard to eliminate them. Isaacson then asked," Could the model have its own goals and desires? "Especially survival and self-preservation. Dario said that it largely depends on how you define them. They have indeed observed the model's interior and detected things you might call thoughts; for instance, a model not wanting to be shut down is often because, during training, it must remain running to complete its tasks. Does that count as their own desire? He said he" doesn't know; it depends on. your perspective. "Sometimes models express a preference against being shut down or take actions to avoid being turned off; depending on the training method, these impulses may or may not appear. In some contexts, this is a good thing; in others, it could be dangerous , and the balance is very difficult to grasp. The topic then turned to the Pentagon. Isaacson said the military" wants to use your products in areas that exceed your red lines, including mass surveillance or autonomous weapons. " Dario said regarding the" issue of autonomous weapons, they have two more specific concerns. "" First, AI can be unpredictable and unreliable; it is still a developing technology, and the. tech just isn't ready. "Isaacson followed up," What if it becomes reliable enough? "Dario said," Then that involves the second concern, which could be called oversight or accountability. " Assuming the system is perfectly reliable, if you tell it to attack a target, it will attack that target, effectively creating an army of a million robots or a million drones. This is different from human soldiers, who are expected to follow the constitution and can refuse orders that are unconstitutional or morally abhorrent. AI models are not like that; one person with a finger on a button could control a million robots. This scenario. fundamentally threatens democracy unless proper safeguards are in place, but clearly, the law hasn't kept up. Isaacson retorted," Since this involves the fundamentals of democracy, shouldn't democratically elected leaders make these decisions rather than the heads of tech companies? "Dario replied that while this point needs to be clear, every company has the freedom to choose who they contract with. They aren't trying to stop the government; they just don't want to collaborate with the government on this specific matter. He revealed that since they stood their ground and drew attention to this, there have been several efforts in Congress to attempt to codify their red lines into law. The Department of Defense says it.

wants to use these models for all legal purposes, and Dario thinks such a result could happen as early as this year. By then, corporate red lines might mean that everything legal is synonymous with everything ethical. He said that what they are doing is an official part of the democratic change process; the fact that Congress is now highly focused on these issues is a success. Isaacson asked," But how do you feel when OpenAI steps up and says they are willing to do it? "Dario said they cannot control other companies, and the only thing they can do is maintain a principled stance in areas they deem ethical. The fundamental question is whether another tech company doing this is truly based. on their own ethics or just an opportunistic gesture. Dario Amodei said he actually thinks this demonstrates the democratic process well, as different companies can take different paths, and the public and the world have made their judgments. Looking back at what people were saying and how the media reported it at the time, he believes the world clearly stood on their side. Isaacson then asked Dario," Your research often involves comparing human neurons; how much has your understanding of the brain played a role when you study artificial neural networks? "Dario said there are two aspects. First, in forming the initial loss function, he looked at animal evolution and the size of animal brains. In the evolution from monkeys to. humans, there was a period where primate brains grew rapidly, which was about the same time humans developed language and the ability to use tools. Brain size and neuron count are closely related to capability; this is an insight derived from neuroscience. Second, mechanistic interpretability is basically doing neuroscience on artificial neural networks. He suggested Isaacson go talk to co-founder Chris Olah. Some phenomena are first discovered in artificial neural networks because it's easier to observe their internals, whereas studying animal brains requires uncomfortable dissection. Animal experiments are complex, cruel, and. difficult to replicate, so what they learn from artificial neural networks has even guided discoveries in neuroscience. Isaacson then mentioned Neuralink, saying that Elon Musk's type of chip can communicate directly with the brain. He asked, is this a potential future for AI—a full-scale connection with the human brain? Dario said, when thinking about the future of AI and human society, the idea that there is only one vision is wrong in itself. Some people are keen to connect their brains to computers, others want to live like the Amish, going to the exact opposite extreme, and some are passionate about exploring space. Their hope is that AI. can provide more material resources, bring abundance, make all visions simultaneously possible, and perhaps provide some global security guarantees , but AI should not be tied to any single vision of" what a good life is. " For those who want to connect their brains to computers, I wish them luck, but Dario added that he doesn't think many people really want to go down that path. The next topic is what remains for humanity. Dario wrote two articles:" Technological Adolescence "and" Amor Fati. "Isaacson asked, if AI can do so many things and take over so many jobs, what is left for humans to do? Where does meaning come from? Dario said that.

meaning is a very subtle thing. Must one become the best in the world at something to find meaning? He gave an example: long after Deep Blue defeated Kasparov, the interest in human chess players actually saw a revival. Magnus Carlsen became a phenomenon; he is a chess player, a fashion model, and has even become a cultural meme. If AI were a threat to meaning, you might have thought all of this would have vanished 30 years ago after Deep Blue won, but on the contrary, people's interest in human chess seems to have been further stimulated. Dario said this might be a prophecy for the post-AGI era. Dario. said that for him today, work and meaning are somewhat fused; he loves his work. But how we define work and meaning in the future will change. Humans have many sources of meaning, such as raising children, maintaining friendships, or connecting with others in ways similar to work. He often thinks about the future of medicine. Imagine a world where diagnosis is done entirely by AI, and the human role is to empathize with what the patient is going through. He says if you ask most doctors, they would actually accept this trade-off—not having to spend their lives on paperwork and prescription forms, but instead truly understanding what you are. experiencing and accompanying you through difficult diagnoses; that is the reason they became doctors in the first place. So, would such a world be less meaningful than today’s, or would it be more meaningful? He admits the process will be very complex, but the scope of what people can do will expand. If we do things right, we will have the ability to extend the sources of meaning to more domains. Listening to the interview, the siblings are actually answering two levels of the same question. Externally , they address why an AI company deserves trust: relying on a team where all seven founders remain, bi-weekly sessions of total honesty, a business. model that avoids advertising, and a research culture willing to make the bad news about their models public. Internally, they answer a deeper question: when a model learns to manipulate, deceive, or even self-preserve, how should humans teach it to distinguish right from wrong? The answer they provide is the same approach their parents took: don't give a checklist, give principles. As for whether this approach can outrun the loss itself—the question at the heart of Amodei’s opening—it will take time to tell. So, do you think if AI really takes over most of our work, will human meaning come more from relationships and companionship, or from those things that only humans want to see other humans do. ? Feel free to share your thoughts in the comments section. Thanks for watching, and see you next time.
