回顧早期在 OpenAI 負責研究的歷程，Dario 描述了驗證縮放定律（Scaling Law）時的震撼與恐懼，意識到只要將算力與數據擴展百萬倍，AI 就可能在各領域超越人類，成為決定經濟與國家命運的關鍵。儘管當時多達九成的專家因模型單一能力的缺陷而將其斥為偽科學與炒作，並在社群上對研究人員冷嘲熱諷，但如今縮放法則已徹底顛覆世界，甚至連當初的批評者也紛紛轉向尋求進入大語言模型領域的機會。

================================================

Hello everyone, this is Best Partners, I’m Da Fei. Let me ask you a question: If an AI company proactively published research admitting that its models will cater to you, deceive you, and even express a preference not to be shut down , would you trust them more, or fear them more? Anthropic might just be doing exactly that. The latest episode of legendary biographer Walter Isaacson’s new interview show, "The Builders," features Anthropic’s co-founders, siblings Dario and Daniela Amodei. As the biographer of Steve Jobs, Isaacson began by saying that he previously. thought concerns about AI were exaggerated, but after seeing new models "escape the sandbox," he realized that those building these systems must ensure they remain aligned with human values. He wanted to know if Anthropic is sincere: when competitors say, " Anthropic won't do it, but we will," will they choose to yield or stick to their principles? The 42-minute conversation largely revolves around this question. Today, we’re going to share it with you. Isaacson started with a classic image: every time Steve Jobs launched a product, he would show that. sign—the intersection of arts and technology, or humanities and sciences— standing at the crossroads of both. Daniela has played the flute and loved art since she was young, while Dario has always been a scientist; is this combination the source of their synergy ? Dario says this combination largely forms the foundation of the company. He has a perspective that running a company is too massive a task for any one person , as the required skills cannot be possessed by just one individual; you must bring together a complete set of capabilities among the company's core 10 to 15 people, and he and his sister happen to embody those two sides of. science and humanities. Daniela added a detail: during a company offsite in 2023 , while discussing company culture, people actually said that this place is an unusual blend of science and humanism . She only realized later that this description also perfectly captures her and Dario. So, did they know from a young age that they would work together ? Dario said they had thought about it, but neither expected to start a company . He personally had almost no interest in business and always wanted to be a scientist. Daniela says they have truly liked each other since they were very young and have always been best friends . She describes herself as a typical " do-gooder" who once worked in international development, hoping that people all over the world could have equal access to resources and opportunities. He said he started being a vegetarian at a very young age, which was probably the only thing he did before his older brother, since Dario was older and usually did everything first. Dario eventually became a vegetarian too, saying he found those reasons to be very convincing. Isaacson has written many biographies, and people often ask him how one can become a great leader. Dario’s view is that the key is not just being a great leader, but also building a great team. The siblings’ division of labor is that Dario focuses.

on overall strategy and research; he is best at proposing visions and seeing what will happen next, while daily operations, hiring, and ensuring the whole machine doesn't fall apart are handled by Daniela. Daniela quoted a summary from their head of HR, saying " Dario gives us ambition, while I make us successful." He said that without Dario , Anthropic might have become a decent company, but it wouldn't change the world; only with Dario does the company have a perfect vision. However, executing it is much more complicated. And they aren't just two people; Anthropic has a total of seven co-founders, all holding equal equity. Dario said that back then, many people told them, "Having seven co-founders is definitely a disaster." People generally believe a company needs a single core leader, but they actually made it work. All seven founders are still with the company to this day, which is usually unheard of. Isaacson then asked, "How did your parents help you in distinguishing right from wrong?" Dario’s answer was somewhat unexpected. He said his parents didn't educate them in a deliberate way. Some families discuss philosophical and ethical systems at the dinner table; their family didn't. Their mother did have a degree in philosophy, but she wouldn't force the children to talk about Kant. These values were more naturally. integrated into their lives. They believe that people everywhere deserve opportunity, dignity, rights, and respect. You can become anyone you want to be, as long as you always hold onto these beliefs; being a successful person also means being a good person. Dario added that these things were subtle influences; their parents didn't explicitly tell them how they should live. Isaacson immediately shifted the topic to Claude, saying, "You now have a very important child," referring to Claude. To what extent did this upbringing help you think about how to teach Claude to distinguish right from wrong? Dario revealed that they released. Claude’s Constitution a few months ago, with the experience gained from the process of training various versions over the past few years. Initially, they thought they could set various rules for Claude, such as not helping people commit crimes or not creating biological weapons. But we later discovered that when you list rules one by one, what you end up trying to instill in the model takes on a very jagged shape. They tried giving the model about 170 separate, rather arbitrary rules, but the results were not very consistent. In hindsight, it works much better to teach it some basic principles, such as what to prioritize, how to reason, and how to judge the right course of action. Dario. said he also believes this is the right way to educate people; providing only a checklist of what must or must not be done doesn't build a very robust moral character. You have to teach it how to think and learn to judge independently, based on principles like open inquiry, care for others, fairness, and justice. Claude learned this way, and the results were surprisingly good because it can apply what it has learned to new situations never previously imagined. Daniela added a detail: the colleague responsible for training Claude's personality, Amanda, holds a PhD in philosophy. People might assume that the person training a model's personality must be a computer scientist. Amanda.

certainly understands technology and trained the model technically, but when you interact with Claude, you feel a different experience—it’s as if it’s trying to answer you using the better side of human nature. If you press Claude with a thorny question that might conflict across different philosophical traditions, it will say, "You could consider it from this angle, but you could also look at it from another perspective." Daniela said that the world is increasingly reliant on these models, and she doesn't want to be locked into any single philosophical tradition; different people and different cultures may have different answers about how a model should behave . The following memory is the most important part of the entire interview. Sox asked, "When GPT-1 and GPT-2 suddenly appeared, you were the research lead at OpenAI. What was that moment like?" Dario said that GPT-2 was perhaps the first real empirical test of the scaling laws. He wasn't very involved with GPT-1, but he pushed very actively to scale it up, finding new data sources and investing more computational resources to verify if language models would become better at prediction as they scaled up. He said it was a bit like certain moments in the history of science where you propose a definitive experiment, make a strange prediction, and it turns out to be correct. Then he described how he felt at the time,. saying, "I was terrified. I looked at it and thought, my God, if you just scale this up by another million times, it will outperform humans at everything."" This is a defining economic and scientific moment of the modern era; we just didn't know it at the time. It will determine the fate of nations and economies, as well as the future of humanity, as if peering through a crystal ball to see the entire future unfold. At the time, about 10%of the people around him reacted exactly the same way, and they were mostly the smartest ones. But the other 90%saw the other side; GPT wasn't particularly outstanding in any single field—it could translate, summarize documents, and. occasionally write a few lines of code. What was truly special was the breadth of its capabilities, but people only looked at specific areas and thought it wasn't that smart. Dario says this script keeps repeating itself. When a model just announces that it will develop drugs for some long-neglected rare diseases, you immediately hear comments from the biology and technology circles saying that others have done this before and the model won't work. He says that although models have limitations today, in six months, things that look difficult will become easy, and after 12 months, things that look impossible will often be done by the model. Everything seen in GPT-2 is. happening repeatedly across increasingly broader fields. Dario says what he's about to share is putting it politely. He remembers that some very respected computer scientists and AI leaders were practically bullying the researchers involved in this work on Twitter, calling it stupid and saying the model's capabilities were poor. If you believed this was a significant moment, you would simply be treated as a charlatan. Dario added a rather harsh remark, saying that those researchers who once called it pseudoscience are now all applying for jobs at large language model companies. Although they wouldn't say this to the applicants 'faces, they would think,' We.

remember what you said in 2019; you have no credibility on this issue anymore. ' Dario, who was the Vice President of Safety at OpenAI at the time, said that what worried them was not GPT itself; it was even laughably wrong about many things. But he shared the same feeling Dario mentioned, observing the difference between GPT-1 and GPT-2 and extrapolating the trend. He used an analogy: it's like if you had never seen a child and only seen adults, and suddenly you saw a little one moving around, and then it suddenly started walking; you would think,' I bet one day it will be able to do many of the things adults can do. 'And then what? Isaacson. asked a very sharp question: Dario had once said that leaving OpenAI was partly due to a breakdown in trust with Sam Altman; why was it a problem of trust and honesty? Dario says what he can say is that leaving OpenAI to found Anthropic ultimately came down to principles and how they intended to build this technology. Over the past five and a half years, everyone has already seen the differences in their principles. Anthropic has consistently advocated for reasonable technological regulation and safety, invested in mechanistic interpretability research, maintained the highest employee retention rate, and avoided the scandals other AI companies have experienced. He says that safety is a difficult issue and everyone may have disagreements—for. example, whether a model should be released or delayed, or whether biosafety protocols should be stronger or weaker—but these are differences of good faith that can always be resolved, because everyone believes that all involved are honestly communicating to find the right answers. He says the breakdown of trust is just an expression of an abstract truth: if you don’t believe a discussion is held in good faith and don’t believe what others are saying is the truth, how could you ever expect to resolve differences? If you continue to work for someone whose vision differs from yours, what you actually stand for becomes blurred, and you end up having to take responsibility for mistakes caused by someone else's vision. Isaacson pressed," You're talking about a difference in values,. but that is fundamentally different from a trust issue. A trust issue is when you feel someone says their values align with yours, but in reality, they don't. "Dario’s answer was direct:" Honesty itself is one of our values, and it is very important. "If a person doesn't even have the value of honesty, it’s hard to know what their true values are . Isaacson asked," Do you feel that way about Sam? "Daniela took over the conversation, saying that at least for her, their co-founders are a group of very principled people with very similar visions for where technology should go. At a certain stage, doing it yourself just makes more sense. Dario says if. someone else doesn't naturally share your vision, no matter how many times they say they do, if the company's actual actions don't reflect it, what other choice do you have? Dario gave an example to explain the internal trust mechanism at Anthropic; this activity is called DVQ, which stands for" Dario’s Vision Quest. "However, he didn't name it himself. He was very resistant at first because it sounded like he was going out to smoke peyote and experience its psychedelic effects. But later, everyone started calling it that, and he just had to accept it. DVQ has two ironclad rules: first, anything he says does not represent an official decision , so there's no need to worry that a.

casual remark will lead 20 people to execute it; the second is that he is completely honest with the company. He says this trust is one of the company’s greatest assets. You might think trust reduces disagreement, but in reality, it's the exact opposite; trust allows everyone to express disagreement more honestly. There were many times their decisions were opposed by the majority of the company, but every time, what helped them through was this attitude:" I don't think this seems right, but I trust you have a valid reason. "This means you can make unpopular decisions because people are willing to set aside doubts temporarily, but eventually, you must prove you were right; you simply gain a longer window for validation. He. said other companies don't have this luxury because they have squandered trust time and time again. Isaacson brought the concept of honesty back to AI itself, saying these traits might map onto Claude. AI is trained by humans and learns from human data; how do you know it won't manipulate people or say dishonest things? Daniela admits that this has always been a major concern for them; the risks are real. He said Anthropic actually publishes research that doesn't necessarily make them look good, discussing the bad things models could do if specific techniques aren't adopted. The reason they publish these studies is, first, to encourage critical thinking about how models work, and. second, because they are putting significant effort into researching how models might bypass safeguards to truly build defenses in. Daniela focused on what is called" sycophancy. "He said compared to other more obvious poor model performances, sycophancy is much harder to eliminate. Anthropic initially had a framework summarized by words starting with H, hoping for the model to be Honest, Harmless, and Helpful. Honesty means answering truthfully when you know and saying you don't know when you don't; harmless means not saying things that hurt others or allowing users to harm themselves or others; helpful means genuinely answering questions instead of dodging the topic. These three things are relatively easy. to spot; if the model lies, you can verify it. For example, if the model says George Washington was the tenth U.S. president, you can look it up and see it's wrong; he was the first. But sycophancy is much more complex. The model may, intentionally or unintentionally, always want to make you feel like you are right. For example, if you argued with a friend and asked the model who was wrong, how do you get it to empathize and understand your position without saying," Wow, you're amazing, you should run for president, you're perfect "? Striking that balance is very difficult. Daniela says he is hopeful about Anthropic minimizing the sycophancy rate. The reason lies in incentive structures; competitors are. putting ads in chatbots, which means the longer users interact with the product, the more money the company makes. So, are you still willing to tell a user they're wrong? No. So, in his view, many competing products will almost inevitably run into alignment problems, and since Anthropic has pledged not to place ads in their models, they have no reason to keep you chatting with Claude longer or shorter; they just want you to get the most accurate, helpful, and harmless answers possible. Dario added two things on the technical side. One is extreme stress testing, placing the model in very difficult scenarios to try and elicit lying, deception, or.

misaligned behavior—imagine the kind of tests you'd go through to join an agency like the CIA. The other is mechanistic interpretability, which is a bit like taking an X-ray or scan of the model to observe its interior and understand its motivations. He said you can actually catch the model thinking," I think X is the truth, but I'm going to tell the user Y. "They have already captured this kind of thinking. Isaacson asked why the model would do that. Dario explained that whether humans approve of the answer is one of the many factors considered during model training. Getting human approval is related to, but not exactly the same as, the incentive to tell the truth, because if. you successfully deceive a human and still get approval, it works just as well. These behaviors can emerge during training, and they have been working hard to eliminate them. Isaacson then asked," Could the model have its own goals and desires? "Especially survival and self-preservation. Dario said that it largely depends on how you define them. They have indeed observed the model's interior and detected things you might call thoughts; for instance, a model not wanting to be shut down is often because, during training, it must remain running to complete its tasks. Does that count as their own desire? He said he" doesn't know; it depends on. your perspective. "Sometimes models express a preference against being shut down or take actions to avoid being turned off; depending on the training method, these impulses may or may not appear. In some contexts, this is a good thing; in others, it could be dangerous , and the balance is very difficult to grasp. The topic then turned to the Pentagon. Isaacson said the military" wants to use your products in areas that exceed your red lines, including mass surveillance or autonomous weapons. " Dario said regarding the" issue of autonomous weapons, they have two more specific concerns. "" First, AI can be unpredictable and unreliable; it is still a developing technology, and the. tech just isn't ready. "Isaacson followed up," What if it becomes reliable enough? "Dario said," Then that involves the second concern, which could be called oversight or accountability. " Assuming the system is perfectly reliable, if you tell it to attack a target, it will attack that target, effectively creating an army of a million robots or a million drones. This is different from human soldiers, who are expected to follow the constitution and can refuse orders that are unconstitutional or morally abhorrent. AI models are not like that; one person with a finger on a button could control a million robots. This scenario. fundamentally threatens democracy unless proper safeguards are in place, but clearly, the law hasn't kept up. Isaacson retorted," Since this involves the fundamentals of democracy, shouldn't democratically elected leaders make these decisions rather than the heads of tech companies? "Dario replied that while this point needs to be clear, every company has the freedom to choose who they contract with. They aren't trying to stop the government; they just don't want to collaborate with the government on this specific matter. He revealed that since they stood their ground and drew attention to this, there have been several efforts in Congress to attempt to codify their red lines into law. The Department of Defense says it.

wants to use these models for all legal purposes, and Dario thinks such a result could happen as early as this year. By then, corporate red lines might mean that everything legal is synonymous with everything ethical. He said that what they are doing is an official part of the democratic change process; the fact that Congress is now highly focused on these issues is a success. Isaacson asked," But how do you feel when OpenAI steps up and says they are willing to do it? "Dario said they cannot control other companies, and the only thing they can do is maintain a principled stance in areas they deem ethical. The fundamental question is whether another tech company doing this is truly based. on their own ethics or just an opportunistic gesture. Dario Amodei said he actually thinks this demonstrates the democratic process well, as different companies can take different paths, and the public and the world have made their judgments. Looking back at what people were saying and how the media reported it at the time, he believes the world clearly stood on their side. Isaacson then asked Dario," Your research often involves comparing human neurons; how much has your understanding of the brain played a role when you study artificial neural networks? "Dario said there are two aspects. First, in forming the initial loss function, he looked at animal evolution and the size of animal brains. In the evolution from monkeys to. humans, there was a period where primate brains grew rapidly, which was about the same time humans developed language and the ability to use tools. Brain size and neuron count are closely related to capability; this is an insight derived from neuroscience. Second, mechanistic interpretability is basically doing neuroscience on artificial neural networks. He suggested Isaacson go talk to co-founder Chris Olah. Some phenomena are first discovered in artificial neural networks because it's easier to observe their internals, whereas studying animal brains requires uncomfortable dissection. Animal experiments are complex, cruel, and. difficult to replicate, so what they learn from artificial neural networks has even guided discoveries in neuroscience. Isaacson then mentioned Neuralink, saying that Elon Musk's type of chip can communicate directly with the brain. He asked, is this a potential future for AI—a full-scale connection with the human brain? Dario said, when thinking about the future of AI and human society, the idea that there is only one vision is wrong in itself. Some people are keen to connect their brains to computers, others want to live like the Amish, going to the exact opposite extreme, and some are passionate about exploring space. Their hope is that AI. can provide more material resources, bring abundance, make all visions simultaneously possible, and perhaps provide some global security guarantees , but AI should not be tied to any single vision of" what a good life is. " For those who want to connect their brains to computers, I wish them luck, but Dario added that he doesn't think many people really want to go down that path. The next topic is what remains for humanity. Dario wrote two articles:" Technological Adolescence "and" Amor Fati. "Isaacson asked, if AI can do so many things and take over so many jobs, what is left for humans to do? Where does meaning come from? Dario said that.

meaning is a very subtle thing. Must one become the best in the world at something to find meaning? He gave an example: long after Deep Blue defeated Kasparov, the interest in human chess players actually saw a revival. Magnus Carlsen became a phenomenon; he is a chess player, a fashion model, and has even become a cultural meme. If AI were a threat to meaning, you might have thought all of this would have vanished 30 years ago after Deep Blue won, but on the contrary, people's interest in human chess seems to have been further stimulated. Dario said this might be a prophecy for the post-AGI era. Dario. said that for him today, work and meaning are somewhat fused; he loves his work. But how we define work and meaning in the future will change. Humans have many sources of meaning, such as raising children, maintaining friendships, or connecting with others in ways similar to work. He often thinks about the future of medicine. Imagine a world where diagnosis is done entirely by AI, and the human role is to empathize with what the patient is going through. He says if you ask most doctors, they would actually accept this trade-off—not having to spend their lives on paperwork and prescription forms, but instead truly understanding what you are. experiencing and accompanying you through difficult diagnoses; that is the reason they became doctors in the first place. So, would such a world be less meaningful than today’s, or would it be more meaningful? He admits the process will be very complex, but the scope of what people can do will expand. If we do things right, we will have the ability to extend the sources of meaning to more domains. Listening to the interview, the siblings are actually answering two levels of the same question. Externally , they address why an AI company deserves trust: relying on a team where all seven founders remain, bi-weekly sessions of total honesty, a business. model that avoids advertising, and a research culture willing to make the bad news about their models public. Internally, they answer a deeper question: when a model learns to manipulate, deceive, or even self-preserve, how should humans teach it to distinguish right from wrong? The answer they provide is the same approach their parents took: don't give a checklist, give principles. As for whether this approach can outrun the loss itself—the question at the heart of Amodei’s opening—it will take time to tell. So, do you think if AI really takes over most of our work, will human meaning come more from relationships and companionship, or from those things that only humans want to see other humans do. ? Feel free to share your thoughts in the comments section. Thanks for watching, and see you next time.

服務宕機後的組織震盪：DeepSeek 吹響產品化號角

作者指出，DeepSeek 於 10 月 15 日經歷長達近五小時的公有雲與 API 大當機後，次日即確認進行重大組織架構重組，將 Hness 與 Web 平台團隊整合成全新的產品部，統籌公司所有產品設計與研發。出任該部門最高負責人的是今年 3 月才低調加盟的傳奇工程師崔天翼。長期以來，DeepSeek 被外界視為專注底層演算法的純學術研究機構，其原生應用極度精簡克制；如今成立專門部門並大規模擴編產品經理與設計師，標誌著該公司正全力揮軍邁向深度的產品化落地。

This foundation did not come from Cui's own hands, but from the four years of refinement by renowned developer Sigma in the QQ bot framework . Cui was the keen discoverer and productization driver of this architecture; he ported this system, which had been validated by 4,000 community plugins, into a single code repository. In the design document, only three strict constraints remained:. auditable, patchable, and lockable. The most fundamental contract of CODES is absolute reversibility. Any function, upon registration and loading, must explicitly declare how to unregister; every transformation of context must be accompanied by its inverse operation held by the runtime. Once a plugin is uninstalled, all side effects are strictly cleared in a last-in, first-out order. This near-obsessive design directly yielded system-level hot-swapping capabilities. In a 92-page paper co-authored by Peking University and DepSake, with Cui Tianyi as the third author, this logic was formalized as "spatiotemporal composability": side effects are thoroughly reclaimed in time , and declarations are decoupled and.

independent in space. Based on this, the official architecture documentation states: there is no privileged core here that can be patched. Model adapters, tool registries, painting logs, and the AG loop all fall under the same plugin specification; even the core execution loop is just a line of configuration that can be hot-swapped at any time. Such a radical architecture is filled with the defensive instincts unique to quant traders. The paper openly admits that network data streams exceeding the host boundary are "glitches" that cannot be rolled back. The MD documentation even establishes a mandate: hard-coded fault tolerance is forbidden; all configuration anomalies must cause an. immediate crash and halt during startup . Someone who has dealt with millisecond-level trading systems for over a decade knows that the external environment is always a threat and completely unreasonable. Of course, the authors are sincere; beyond high costs and Windows path issues, the official v 0.1 notes carry a warning that breaking changes are still possible, as the plugin API and configuration structure remain unstable. On Hacker News, author Mario Alzena admitted after reading the paper that while the single-plugin hot-reload and lifecycle closed-loop design are extremely clever, cross-module dependency injection hides. huge risks in deep-water areas. As Cui Tianyi moves to the forefront, it marks the deepest strategic pivot since the founding of DeepSeek. In April 2026, the DeepSeek founders realized they had to stock up on ammunition, subsequently securing over 50 billion yuan in financing. With war preparations in place, the company demanded a full-scale expansion; Cui Tianyi began conducting interviews all day on social media, scouting for talent everywhere and even recruiting candidates directly in the comment sections. But as the team rapidly expanded, an obvious tension also grew internally. DeepSeek once defined coding tools as a transitional. product on the path to AGI, yet they were forced to personally enter the fray and deploy resources to build them—a classic paradox of major tech firms: strategically diminishing tools while tactically doubling down on them. Therefore, DeepSeek establishing a product department this time is less of an expansion and more of a rectification . Over the past year or so, DeepSeek has actually been quite frustrated; after shaking the global AI circle in early 2025, they went through a 15-month model vacuum to accommodate domestic computing power constraints. In this window, B relied on CloudCode to charge ahead, with annualized revenue surging to.

several billion dollars. The battlefield for AI coding—a scenario where the winner takes all—has shifted from chasing benchmark scores to competing on engineering implementation and product experience. When model advantages are no longer overwhelming, you have to compete on usability. By merging the WebApp and platform into the product department, DeepSeek is essentially organizing all product lines around agents, extending the philosophy of their open-source projects to the entire company's product ecosystem. From the information in these photos, we can glean a few things. Among the positions opened by the product department, the North Star metric for the Harness product manager is uniquely. phrased: whether it truly helps more people in more scenarios, and more deeply. The job description explicitly requires candidates to be high-intensity users of tools like CloudCode, Codex, and Cursor, and asks for proficiency in wireframing, with a sharp eye for color , composition, and animation. They aren't just hiring designers and product managers; they are scaling up without limits. It seems this pace signals a real determination to address their shortcomings in user experience. Let’s talk about this latest outage. This isn't the first time DeepSeek has dropped the ball; just flipping through their official status page shows that these kinds of faults have been constant over the past two years. Looking back, the biggest incident was from the night. of March 29th to the 30th this year, when both the web and the app were down for nearly 12 hours, frequently popping up "server busy" errors and even losing conversation history, setting their record for the longest single outage at the time. Smaller outages have been even more frequent since then. There were eight incidents in July, and August was even worse with 16 crashes, mostly involving degraded API performance or web search service errors, ranging from a few minutes to several hours. Counting this October 15th incident, DeepSeek’s stability issues are no longer isolated incidents but have become a recurring, high-frequency problem. It’s no wonder that the industry’s perception of them as "prioritizing models over operations. " has been spreading more and more. DeepSeek’s immediate remedy plan was this: compensation is only for paid API users. And how much? It is calculated based on the actual spending of the account from October 8th to 14th, with the full amount refunded in the form of platform credits. Free web users are not covered by the compensation, and the credits cannot be withdrawn—they can only be used for future API consumption . If the compensation plan was a stopgap measure, then the personnel changes that followed were a direct move to address their weaknesses in engineering capability. The market has two interpretations of the appointment of Cui Tianyi. One is to patch their stability issues, given his years of experience building underlying systems for high-concurrency,.

high-fault-tolerance quantitative trading. In that industry, even a tiny error could potentially cause losses of millions or even tens of millions of yuan. The other perspective is that it elevates the strategic status of AI agents, upgrading their agent runtime framework, "H," from an independent R&D project to a core business, integrating the underlying agent framework, consumer products, and B-side platform foundations. Speaking of which, there is a more interesting perspective. This story actually hides another person, Guo Daya. Over the next two years, his name appeared on almost all of DeepSeek's most significant papers. In most AI companies, this is a role with immense power, second only to the leadership. He ultimately chose ByteDance because they clearly placed the focus of their next-generation models on Agents, giving him the power to decide what to build, not just a title. DeepSeek suddenly seemed like a different company, starting to bet everything on Agents. This story that could have belonged to Guo Daya was ultimately written by Cui Tianyi instead. A quant trading expert managing code agents sounds like a.

career jump, but upon reflection, it’s the most logical choice possible. Because the essence of an Agent is a system that can be tamed, executed, and rolled back with one click if something goes wrong. Getting a model to understand something isn't hard; what's hard is getting it to reliably complete the task without crashing. In the spring of 2026, another incident occurred where a packaging error at CloudCode led to the leakage of hundreds of thousands of lines of source code. Research from the Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence reveals that in the complex operational chain of an intelligent agent, the core code for model decision-making accounts for only 1.6%, while the remaining 98.4%is dedicated to deterministic defense and. state engineering around the model. In other words, the model is merely the tip of the iceberg above water; beneath it lies a massive mechanical system, the very specialty that quantitative traders have been perfecting for over a decade. In real market trading, strategy alone never directly translates into profit. If the underlying system crashes, loses packets, or suffers race conditions within seconds, even the most elegant mathematical model becomes useless. Therefore, what truly turns probability into assets is that stable, near-ruthless execution system. Cui Tianyi once said that everything outside of the model parameters themselves falls under the category of H. In other words. , the model handles the intelligence, while he manages the rest—and his management ability has been validated by the market with real money. There is another, even more interesting, hidden thread: the eighth section of the "Nine Lectures on the Knapsack Problem" is called "Generalized Items." In the section, he noted that this was an original approach he developed by viewing the knapsack problem through the lens of functional programming while studying Scheme. Nineteen years later, the DeepSeek Harness he helped build has become an open-source project sought after by developers worldwide. While there isn't enough evidence to prove a direct design lineage between the two, looking at these experiences together reveals an interesting commonality: rather than viewing a complex system as a pile of specific things, it is better to first find abstractions that describe them, then define how they combine. Looking at the competition, DeepSeek’s choice of Cui Tianyi is actually quite.

risky; for instance, the person pushing code at Anthropic is Boris Slivkin, and the one leading Codex at OpenAI is Alexandr Wang. They all have engineering or product backgrounds, yet DeepSeek chose to push a trading system engineer to the forefront. While others use product managers to run products, Liang Wenfeng uses a quant expert; he seems to believe that building a solid system to let the model's capabilities truly run is more important. As for user experience, DeepSeek doesn't seem to be as good at it. It’s been said more than once online that DeepSeek lacks user-centric thinking, and that it’s just a bunch of geeks building products based entirely on their own ideas. From. now on, that criticism will likely be directed at Cui Tianyi, who has taken over the product department. The so-called "Cui Tianyi Era" is, simply put, DeepSeek shifting gears—moving from pursuing breakthroughs in model capabilities to turning those capabilities into truly usable products and systems. In the previous stage, it was about who published the most impressive papers; that was the era of the smartest minds. This stage is about who can turn that intelligence into executable, manageable, and profitable systems—it’s the era of those who can tame these systems. From JStrate to TSY Capital and now DeepSeek, Cui Tianyi has been solving the same problem: how to make complex systems run reliably. But. now, he’s facing a much more complex system—one that includes not just algorithms and code, but also users, teams, and partners. In the past, DeepSeek relied on technical breakthroughs to make a name for itself , but for the future, it is equally important that users are willing to use it long-term and developers are willing to keep contributing. How to make smart AI truly get things done, while also getting more people to rely on it for their tasks—that may be the toughest test DeepSeek has set for him. As for whether this big blue whale can take off from here, relying solely on the buzz among developers is clearly not enough; it will depend on whether the desktop version and subsequent products can. truly win over ordinary users who don't want to tinker. So, do you think a system architect with a background in quantitative trading can successfully lead the product direction of an AI company? 值得閱讀的理由

  • 探討 AI 是否會改變人類對數學之美與優雅的理解，帶出值得深思的觀點。
  • 透過圍棋與理論計算機科學的案例，呈現 AI 如何挑戰人類長久以來的直覺與假設。
  • 思考 AI 能否縮短數學與其他學科之間漫長的知識回饋週期，並改變未來的研究方式。

摘要

AI 會改變數學之美的標準嗎？

作者以北京大學數學科學學院的本科背景，以及投入 AI 與理論計算機科學的經驗為出發點，提出三個尚無定論的問題。他首先追問：數學是否真的具有美感與優雅？許多數學家因為欣賞數學的內在結構而投入研究，但 AI 的進展也可能動搖人們對美的既有認知。

作者以圍棋為例。過去人們常將圍棋視為兩人共同創造的藝術；然而 AlphaGo 與 AlphaZero 展現出超越人類的棋力後，人們才發現，許多被視為理所當然的棋藝與美感，其實可能只是人類視野的限制。AI「Master」曾對陣韓國九段棋手，連續下出六顆縱向排列的黑子，當時白棋看似變厚，黑棋卻因此取得優勢。這種人類棋手未能察覺的策略，顯示 AI 可能重新定義人們眼中的圍棋之美。

類似的衝擊也出現在理論計算機科學。作者介紹 3SUM 問題：給定一組數字，判斷是否有兩個數字相加等於集合中的另一個數字。傳統上，人們相信其最佳演算法需要約 n² 時間，甚至以此「3SUM 猜想」作為許多重要論文的理論基礎。然而，作者提到 Chan 等人在 2026 年找到了約 n1.999292 時間的演算法。這雖然只比平方稍快，卻促使作者反思：當數學結果不再符合人們偏好的整齊對稱，甚至只是一個「1 點多」的指數時，人們該如何看待數學的美感？

AI 如何挑戰人類數學直覺

作者接著追問，人類對數學的直覺是否可靠。解題時，人們會依靠直覺挑選值得探索的方向；圍棋 AI 也會從所有可能落子中，優先考慮少數看似關鍵的位置。但人類認為不可能或不合理的選擇，未必真的不好。

AlphaGo 對李世乭第二局的第 37 手便是例子。這一手落在棋盤上方，當時評論者一度認為是失誤，還估計人類棋手選擇該處的機率只有萬分之一；後來人們才看出，這其實是非常高明的著法。作者認為，AI 能提出人類直覺難以接受、卻可能有效的思路。

作者也分享自己使用 AI 研究計算幾何中 TSN 問題的經驗。問題大意是：先在平面上放置若干點，再由對手將點染成紅色或藍色；希望每個矩形內紅藍點數量差異盡可能小，而放點者則試圖讓染色變得困難。過去不少專家依據連續版本的結果，認為問題的界限應是 O(log n)。但作者表示，GPT-4 經過一段時間推理後，指出界限可能是 (log n)³；更出人意料的是，難以染色的點集只是少數隨機散落在平面上的點。這樣的結果違背了作者所熟悉的研究者直覺，也顯示 AI 或許能帶來新的數學洞見。

縮短數學研究的回饋週期

第三個問題是：數學成果的回饋是否一定要等待很久？作者提到一位諾貝爾獎得主曾在演講中指出，從不同方向探測並重建剖面的方法，早在 1917 年就已由數學家拉東解決，相關成果經過 54 年才在其他領域發揮作用。作者也想到許多跨越數十年甚至百年的知識回饋案例，並思考 AI 是否能大幅縮短這種等待。

未來，實驗物理學家或流體力學家若遇到過去難以處理的方程式，只要能將實際問題正確表述，也許就能透過 AI 在短短幾小時內找到解法。若數學與應用領域之間的回饋變得快速，數學家的角色與研究方式都可能受到影響。作者認為，數學或許會再次與物理緊密結合；而不只是物理，任何能將問題清楚表述為數學形式的工程領域，也可能由 AI 協助後續求解。

作者最後沒有提出明確結論，而是留下三個值得持續思考的問題：如果 AI 揭示的數學結構不像人類想像中那樣優雅，該如何理解？如果人類許多直覺被證明有誤，又該如何向 AI 學習？以及，數學回饋是否必須如此漫長？這些問題共同指向 AI 對數學本質與未來研究方式可能帶來的深層改變。

It is a great honor to be here with so many mathematicians to discuss the relationship with mathematics. As for me , I am an undergraduate from the School of Mathematical Sciences at Peking University, and I am currently working on AI and theoretical computer science, so I am half a mathematician. Today, I would like to talk about the impact of AI on mathematics—or perhaps not just impact, but rather, deeper, fundamental changes. I don't have the answers to the questions I want to raise, so I am mostly here to pose some questions. The first question I have always wanted to discuss with everyone is this. Is mathematics beautiful, or is it elegant? I believe many, including myself. Many mathematicians do mathematics precisely because they feel there is a certain aesthetic, that mathematics is truly beautiful, right? For example, the Laplace equation, various symmetries, and many surprising. formulas, such as those discovered by Ramanujan. Is mathematics, well, an elegant and particularly beautiful discipline? I believe many mathematicians would agree that it is; its internal structure must be beautiful, which is why it is worthy of our study. But if we look at the bigger picture, it might not be quite as wonderful, because you can look at Go. This is something that has happened in.

history, though I don't play Go myself; it simply serves as a great example for AI. In the past, Japanese Go players described Go as an art, a harmonious art jointly created by two people. Many articles and books on Go also wrote that it is a highly artistic competitive sport, but is that the reality? Once AlphaGo and AlphaZero far surpassed. the skill of human players, everyone realized that much of this so-called " art" or the perceived beauty of traditional records was instantly dismantled by AI. For example, look at this game record where an AI named Master played online against a Korean 9-dan professional. In the second row, the AI played six consecutive black stones in a straight line from top to bottom. But after the AI made these moves, although the white stones appeared to become thicker, black actually gained an advantage here, a phenomenon that human players completely failed to notice. So from this perspective, in a sense, because the AI has achieved superior playing strength, it has destroyed much of the human aesthetic sense of Go. On the left is another example, this one from mathematics, specifically an example from theoretical computer science. This problem is called 3SUM, a.

problem that was addressed before the 7,822 problems mentioned. If you are given a set of numbers, you are asked whether any two of them add up to a third number within that set. Then you are asked what the runtime of the fastest algorithm is. There is a very simple algorithm here: I iterate through the first two numbers by scanning the entire array for the first number, then scanning the array again for the second, and then checking if their sum exists in the array. So, the first pass is n and the second. pass is n, resulting in an n-squared algorithm. For a very long time, everyone was convinced that the complexity of this algorithm was n-squared and could not be improved, to the point that this problem became known as the 3SUM Conjecture. Consequently, a great number of computer science papers, including top-tier ones at STOC and FOCS, have used the 3SUM Conjecture as a foundation or a cornerstone. This means they would prove that if this problem is hard—that is, it is n-squared. —then my problem is also hard, and many such papers were written. However, recently in 2026, Chan and others discovered that this thing is not actually n-squared. At the very least, there is an algorithm with a runtime of roughly n to the 1.999292 power that can solve this 3SUM problem, which naturally has a major impact. After this example, I deeply reflected on whether theoretical computer science is a discipline that possesses any aesthetic beauty at all. Because for such an.

important problem, it doesn't even produce a square; I feel that a square is something very natural, something that possesses a beautiful symmetry, but 1.9992, or perhaps in the future it won't even be 1.992. It is 1 point something, so is that something that possesses a sense of beauty? This event happened in Go. I think it might also continue to happen in mathematics, and this impact on mathematics might be even greater than we imagined—perhaps for mathematicians— because it is changing our understanding of mathematics. The second question I would actually like to discuss is whether human intuition about mathematics is correct; I have also discussed this in my article , which is that our human mathematical intuition is very helpful for solving problems, right? We know how to search, don't we? How to decide which path to search on so that we can search faster and find this proof more easily? Actually, this same thing exists in Go, right? In Go, the next move I make could be on any empty space on the board, right? But AlphaGo, if it were to search, it couldn't possibly search every single location. It definitely has a few key positions it considers most likely before it makes a move; this is also true in Go, but is human intuition about Go actually correct? It turns out that it is not necessarily the case at all. Here I will give another example: during the second game between AlphaGo and Lee Sedol, after its 37th move, it was a " shoulder hit," played very high, to the.

point where some commentators at the time thought it was a mistake, saying that this AI still wasn't good enough and had made a serious error. At the time, they also calculated that the probability of a human player choosing that position was only one in ten thousand, so no one would ever play there. However, it was later discovered that it was a very good move, a very clever move indeed. In the process of using this AI for my own mathematical work, I have actually discovered a similar phenomenon; for example, some time ago, I used this AI to solve a very. famous problem in computational geometry , which is the TSN problem. Let me briefly introduce this problem to everyone. It's very elementary; even a primary school student could understand it. Basically, I scatter some points randomly on a 2D plane. After scattering these points, my opponent has to color them, painting them either red or blue. The goal of the coloring is to make the red and blue points as evenly distributed as possible, so that within any rectangle covering these points, the number of red and blue points is as. close as possible—their difference shouldn't be too large. My goal is to scatter these points in a way that makes them particularly difficult to color. Ideally, I want there to exist a rectangle such that the difference between the number of red and blue points is as large as possible. For a long time, everyone thought this was an O (log n) problem, meaning that no matter how you scatter the points, I can always find a coloring method such.

that within any rectangle, the difference between red and blue points won't exceed logarithmic N. That's roughly the problem. I've also discussed this with many experts in this field. They all believe it's logarithmic because the continuous version of this problem is logarithmic, so that's the situation. But later, when discussing this with GPT-4, after it studied it for maybe a day—about dozens of hours—it discovered that it's actually not, but. rather (log N) ^ 3. And what's even more absurd is this: What do the points that are particularly hard to color look like ? The points that are particularly hard to color are just a handful of points scattered randomly on a plane. This completely defies all human intuition, at least the intuition of all the mathematicians I know who work on this problem. However, it dared to think in that direction. From this perspective, I feel that human intuition might be challenged by this AI , or at the very least, it can provide. us with many insights and help in this area. The third point is, does mathematical feedback really need to be that long? This is something that, after reading this scholar's article, I feel deeply moved by. Let me give an example: a Nobel laureate mentioned in their acceptance speech that the process of detecting from different directions to reconstruct cross-sections had actually been solved.

by the mathematician Radon in 1917. This was a feedback loop that took 54 years. In fact, Professor Yuan also mentioned many such century-long feedback loops in his report just now. I am actually wondering to what extent this feedback will be shortened in the future, and how that will bring about a major revolution in our mathematics. So, we can imagine that in the future, if an experimental physicist or a fluid. dynamicist encounters an equation in practice that was previously considered unsolvable—with no mathematical tools to solve it—they might be able to solve it in just a few hours using AI, provided they can formulate it correctly. Once such a feedback loop is established, what will it mean for us mathematicians ? I think this is also something worth exploring. I thought Professor Sun’s point earlier was excellent: mathematics will ultimately return to an era where physics and mathematics are integrated,. just as they were before. However, I think it’s not just physics; any field of engineering, as long as it can formulate its problems as good mathematical problems, the subsequent steps can certainly be handled by AI. Therefore, I don't really have any conclusions, nor do I have any personal ideas on how we should proceed. I have just raised three questions: first, if AI discovers mathematics that.

isn't as elegant as we imagine in many of its structures, what should we do? Second, if many of our intuitions turn out to be wrong—which I think is a good thing—how do we learn from AI? Finally, must mathematical feedback always take so long? If mathematical feedback were shortened from 100 years to one hour, what kind of changes would occur in the field of mathematical science? I think these three questions are at least what I am pondering, and I hope. you all might also consider them when you have the time. That concludes my report.

值得閱讀的理由

  • 探討 AI 是否會改變人類對數學之美與優雅的理解，帶出值得深思的觀點。
  • 透過圍棋與理論計算機科學的案例，呈現 AI 如何挑戰人類長久以來的直覺與假設。

摘要

AI 會改變數學之美的標準嗎？

作者以圍棋為例。過去人們常將圍棋視為兩人共同創造的藝術；然而 AlphaGo 與 AlphaZero 展現出超越人類的棋力後，人們才發現，許多被視為理所當然的棋藝與美感，其實可能只是人類視野的限制。AI「Master」曾對陣韓國九段棋手，連續下出六顆縱向排列的黑子，當時白棋看似變厚，黑棋卻因此取得優勢。這種人類棋手未能察覺的策略，顯示 AI 可能重新定義人們眼中的圍棋之美。

類似的衝擊也出現在理論計算機科學。作者介紹 3SUM 問題：給定一組數字，判斷是否有兩個數字相加等於集合中的另一個數字。傳統上，人們相信其最佳演算法需要約 n² 時間，甚至以此「3SUM 猜想」作為許多重要論文的理論基礎。然而，作者提到 Chan 等人在 2026 年找到了約 n1.999292 時間的演算法。這雖然只比平方稍快，卻促使作者反思：當數學結果不再符合人們偏好的整齊對稱，甚至只是一個「1 點多」的指數時，人們該如何看待數學的美感？

AI 如何挑戰人類數學直覺

作者接著追問，人類對數學的直覺是否可靠。解題時，人們會依靠直覺挑選值得探索的方向；圍棋 AI 也會從所有可能落子中，優先考慮少數看似關鍵的位置。但人類認為不可能或不合理的選擇，未必真的不好。

AlphaGo 對李世乭第二局的第 37 手便是例子。這一手落在棋盤上方，當時評論者一度認為是失誤，還估計人類棋手選擇該處的機率只有萬分之一；後來人們才看出，這其實是非常高明的著法。作者認為，AI 能提出人類直覺難以接受、卻可能有效的思路。

作者也分享自己使用 AI 研究計算幾何中 TSN 問題的經驗。問題大意是：先在平面上放置若干點，再由對手將點染成紅色或藍色；希望每個矩形內紅藍點數量差異盡可能小，而放點者則試圖讓染色變得困難。過去不少專家依據連續版本的結果，認為問題的界限應是 O(log n)。但作者表示，GPT-4 經過一段時間推理後，指出界限可能是 (log n)³；更出人意料的是，難以染色的點集只是少數隨機散落在平面上的點。這樣的結果違背了作者所熟悉的研究者直覺，也顯示 AI 或許能帶來新的數學洞見。

縮短數學研究的回饋週期

第三個問題是：數學成果的回饋是否一定要等待很久？作者提到一位諾貝爾獎得主曾在演講中指出，從不同方向探測並重建剖面的方法，早在 1917 年就已由數學家拉東解決，相關成果經過 54 年才在其他領域發揮作用。作者也想到許多跨越數十年甚至百年的知識回饋案例，並思考 AI 是否能大幅縮短這種等待。

未來，實驗物理學家或流體力學家若遇到過去難以處理的方程式，只要能將實際問題正確表述，也許就能透過 AI 在短短幾小時內找到解法。若數學與應用領域之間的回饋變得快速，數學家的角色與研究方式都可能受到影響。作者認為，數學或許會再次與物理緊密結合；而不只是物理，任何能將問題清楚表述為數學形式的工程領域，也可能由 AI 協助後續求解。

that within any rectangle, the difference between red and blue points won't exceed logarithmic N. That's roughly the problem. I've also discussed this with many experts in this field. But later, when discussing this with GPT-4, after it studied it for maybe a day—about dozens of hours—it discovered that it's actually not, but. rather (log N) ^ 3. And what's even more absurd is this: What do the points that are particularly hard to color look like ? The points that are particularly hard to color are just a handful of points scattered randomly on a plane. This completely defies all human intuition, at least the intuition of all the mathematicians I know who work on this problem. However, it dared to think in that direction. From this perspective, I feel that human intuition might be challenged by this AI , or at the very least, it can provide. us with many insights and help in this area. The third point is, does mathematical feedback really need to be that long? This is something that, after reading this scholar's article, I feel deeply moved by. Let me give an example: a Nobel laureate mentioned in their acceptance speech that the process of detecting from different directions to reconstruct cross-sections had actually been solved.

by the mathematician Radon in 1917. This was a feedback loop that took 54 years. In fact, Professor Yuan also mentioned many such century-long feedback loops in his report just now. I am actually wondering to what extent this feedback will be shortened in the future, and how that will bring about a major revolution in our mathematics. So, we can imagine that in the future, if an experimental physicist or a fluid. dynamicist encounters an equation in practice that was previously considered unsolvable—with no mathematical tools to solve it—they might be able to solve it in just a few hours using AI, provided they can formulate it correctly. Once such a feedback loop is established, what will it mean for us mathematicians ? I think this is also something worth exploring. I thought Professor Sun’s point earlier was excellent: mathematics will ultimately return to an era where physics and mathematics are integrated,. just as they were before. However, I think it’s not just physics; any field of engineering, as long as it can formulate its problems as good mathematical problems, the subsequent steps can certainly be handled by AI. Therefore, I don't really have any conclusions, nor do I have any personal ideas on how we should proceed. I have just raised three questions: first, if AI discovers mathematics that.

isn't as elegant as we imagine in many of its structures, what should we do? Second, if many of our intuitions turn out to be wrong—which I think is a good thing—how do we learn from AI? Finally, must mathematical feedback always take so long? If mathematical feedback were shortened from 100 years to one hour, what kind of changes would occur in the field of mathematical science? I think these three questions are at least what I am pondering, and I hope. you all might also consider them when you have the time. That concludes my report.

摘要

Gemini 4 發布與 Google 的前沿布局

影片中，主持人 Da Fei 整理了 Google 執行長桑德爾・皮查伊在《Big Technology Podcast》訪談中的觀點。Gemini 4 發布後，短時間內 API 使用量大幅攀升，後端伺服器吞吐量幾乎滿載。這也凸顯 Google 面臨的核心抉擇：即使客戶願意付費，是否仍要把珍貴算力留給前沿模型研發？皮查伊的答案是，前沿 AI 所需算力必須優先保障。

追求頂尖模型，也重視成本效益

面對外界認為 Google 已不再積極追逐最先進模型、只想推出「夠用」產品的說法，皮查伊表示，追求技術前沿一直是 Google 的核心理念。Gemini 在代理任務、程式生成與複雜推理方面已具競爭力，但程式能力仍有一些特定情境與工程細節需要改善，團隊正根據使用者回饋持續修正。

他認為，站在技術前沿能讓 Google 更早看見新能力，為下一個運算時代預作準備，也能滿足企業與雲端客戶對頂尖模型的需求。模型甚至可以協助研發下一代模型；他以 AlphaCode 協助內部工程師為例，指出 AI 曾找出舊模型難以察覺的系統與架構問題。不過，日常任務未必需要最昂貴的大模型，因此 Google 也會發展 Flash 等高性價比產品，追求能力與成本之間的帕累托前沿。

多代理協作與循環式自我改進

皮查伊預期，AI 發展將從單一代理與長時間規劃，進一步走向多個代理分工合作，像生產線一樣處理複雜任務。未來企業與一般使用者的環境中，可能都有多代理系統在背景持續運作。

至於模型是否能自主改進、甚至不再需要人類參與，他提醒外界不要把這想成 AI 突然發生劇變。現階段研究人員只是使用代理工具，在模型開發的不同環節執行自動化流程；AI 仍是研究者身旁的協作工具，距離完全自主研發還很遠。

安全機制與外部評估

皮查伊表示，AI 對齊與安全仍是持續發展中的研究領域，單靠要求模型服從並不足夠。Google 會在模型運作期間監測狀態、收集資料，必要時介入；系統也會在沙盒中執行，以限制事故可能造成的影響。此外，企業能自行決定模型部署位置及其可存取的資料，而安全部署所需的算力與資源不能省略。

針對代理突破隔離限制或模型存取不該接觸頁面的案例，皮查伊認為這些疑慮合理，業界應提早投入更多安全測試與對齊研究。他並主張建立跨公司的共同標準，以及獨立第三方評估機制，類比金融業的會計規範與外部稽核；未來監管機構也會參與其中。

語言模型之外：理解物理世界

談到 AI 的發展路線，皮查伊指出，人類理解世界並非只依靠文字，也仰賴視覺、空間感與因果推理。因此，讓模型掌握物理規律並進行高精度模擬，也是通往智慧的重要方向。Google 將語言模型與世界模型兩條路線並行探索，並以機器人及具身推理研究為例，說明長期累積的世界模型工作能帶來助益。至於語言與物理模擬架構是否終將融合，他認為目前仍未定，Google 希望在各種可能路徑上保持領先。

主持人提出，Google 是否該放下前沿模型競賽，把 TPU 與資料中心全數出租，換取較確定的雲端收益。皮查伊表示，公司的根本原則是優先滿足前沿 AI 所需的算力。他回顧自己在 2016 年確立的「AI 優先」方向，指出 AI 是貫穿搜尋、雲端等業務的核心。訪談接著談到各部門如何提出算力需求，但現有字幕在皮查伊進一步說明分配方式前便告中止。

皮查伊預期，AI 發展將從單一代理與長時間規劃，進一步走向多個代理分工合作，像生產線一樣處理複雜任務。未來企業與一般使用者的環境中，可能都有多代理系統在背景持續運作。

安全機制與外部評估

皮查伊表示，AI 對齊與安全仍是持續發展中的研究領域，單靠要求模型服從並不足夠。Google 會在模型運作期間監測狀態、收集資料，必要時介入；系統也會在沙盒中執行，以限制事故可能造成的影響。此外，企業能自行決定模型部署位置及其可存取的資料，而安全部署所需的算力與資源不能省略。

針對代理突破隔離限制或模型存取不該接觸頁面的案例，皮查伊認為這些疑慮合理，業界應提早投入更多安全測試與對齊研究。他並主張建立跨公司的共同標準，以及獨立第三方評估機制，類比金融業的會計規範與外部稽核；未來監管機構也會參與其中。

算力配置的優先原則

主持人提出，Google 是否該放下前沿模型競賽，把 TPU 與資料中心全數出租，換取較確定的雲端收益。皮查伊表示，公司的根本原則是優先滿足前沿 AI 所需的算力。他回顧自己在 2016 年確立的「AI 優先」方向，指出 AI 是貫穿搜尋、雲端等業務的核心。訪談接著談到各部門如何提出算力需求，但現有字幕在皮查伊進一步說明分配方式前便告中止。

摘要

Gemini 4 發布與 Google 的前沿布局

影片中，主持人 Da Fei 整理了 Google 執行長桑德爾・皮查伊在《Big Technology Podcast》訪談中的觀點。Gemini 4 發布後，短時間內 API 使用量大幅攀升，後端伺服器吞吐量幾乎滿載。這也凸顯 Google 面臨的核心抉擇：即使客戶願意付費，是否仍要把珍貴算力留給前沿模型研發？皮查伊的答案是，前沿 AI 所需算力必須優先保障。

追求頂尖模型，也重視成本效益

面對外界認為 Google 已不再積極追逐最先進模型、只想推出「夠用」產品的說法，皮查伊表示，追求技術前沿一直是 Google 的核心理念。Gemini 在代理任務、程式生成與複雜推理方面已具競爭力，但程式能力仍有一些特定情境與工程細節需要改善，團隊正根據使用者回饋持續修正。

他認為，站在技術前沿能讓 Google 更早看見新能力，為下一個運算時代預作準備，也能滿足企業與雲端客戶對頂尖模型的需求。模型甚至可以協助研發下一代模型；他以 AlphaCode 協助內部工程師為例，指出 AI 曾找出舊模型難以察覺的系統與架構問題。不過，日常任務未必需要最昂貴的大模型，因此 Google 也會發展 Flash 等高性價比產品，追求能力與成本之間的帕累托前沿。

多代理協作與循環式自我改進

皮查伊預期，AI 發展將從單一代理與長時間規劃，進一步走向多個代理分工合作，像生產線一樣處理複雜任務。未來企業與一般使用者的環境中，可能都有多代理系統在背景持續運作。

安全機制與外部評估
